Cozy Halloween Beanie - Quick Crochet Pattern

This cozy Halloween beanie has been my favorite quick spooky make this October — chunky, warm, and just a little playful with those black and pumpkin stripes. I love wearing it for chilly morning walks with coffee, pumpkin patch trips, and of course trick-or-treating with the kids.

It's beginner-friendly, made from a simple rectangle that we seam into a beanie — no working in the round to start, no complicated decreases. If you can chain and half double crochet, you can make this. I used black and pumpkin orange super chunky yarn and an 8mm hook, so it works up in about an hour. The bat detail on mine is optional — I just crocheted a tiny bat and sewed it on, but it looks cute even without it.

Skill level Beginner — rectangle beanie, no crown shaping in round
Hook 8 mm crochet hook
Yarn Super chunky / bulky — black + pumpkin orange

Before you begin — how this beanie is built

I used to think beanies had to be crocheted in the round from the top down with lots of increasing and decreasing. This one is different and much easier for beginners. We crochet a flat rectangle, about 10 inches tall and 18 inches wide. Then we fold it in half, seam one side to make a tube, and cinch the top closed to form the crown. That's it. No circle, no magic ring needed to start.

Think of it like this: the chain edge is the height of your beanie from brim to crown. The rows you add are the width that wraps around your head. My rectangle is 32 chains tall (about 10 inches) and 38 rows wide (about 18 inches when flat). When you seam the 10-inch sides together, the 18-inch width becomes the circumference around your head — about 19-20 inches relaxed, stretching to 22 inches. Fits most adults.

Because we use super chunky yarn, it grows fast and the texture looks like little pumpkins all lined up, especially when you switch between black and pumpkin orange every 4 rows. If you are brand new, keep a stitch marker in your first stitch of each row — chunky yarn can be hard to count at first.

Tip from my table: I like to chain a little loosely. If your foundation chain is too tight, your brim will be tight. Go up to 9mm hook just for the chain if you tend to crochet tight, then switch back to 8mm for the rows. And count your stitches after row 1 — you should have 31 hdc. If you have 30 or 32, it's easier to fix now than 20 rows later.

Materials I used

  • Super chunky yarn: About 120 yards total. I used black (about 60 yards) and pumpkin orange (about 60 yards). I used Lion Brand Wool-Ease Thick & Quick or similar — acrylic wool blend, soft, warm, holds shape. One skein of each color is more than enough. For the little bat, I used a scrap of black, about 2 yards.
  • 8mm crochet hook: My go-to for chunky beanies. Keeps fabric soft, not stiff. Bamboo or ergonomic handle is nice for chunky yarn.
  • Tapestry needle: Big eye, for seaming the side and cinching the crown. I like the bent-tip ones for chunky yarn.
  • Scissors, stitch marker, measuring tape: Nothing fancy — a locking marker to mark row 1.
  • Optional bat: Small amount of black yarn, 4mm hook if you want a tiny bat applique like mine. Or use a felt bat like in the pin — both cute.

Sizing & how to measure your head

This beanie is written for adult S/M — about 19-20 inches around relaxed, stretches comfortably to 22 inches, and about 10 inches tall with a little slouch. My head is 21 inches and it fits with a cozy stretch.

  • How to measure: Wrap a soft tape around your head where you like your beanie to sit — right above eyebrows and over ears. That's your head circumference.
  • Flat rectangle: Chain 32 = 10 inches tall (brim to crown). 38 rows = 18 inches wide flat. When seamed into a tube, 18 inches becomes about 19 inches around relaxed because seaming adds a tiny bit and chunky stretches. So if your head is 21 inches, you want finished beanie 19-20 inches relaxed for a snug cozy fit.
  • To adjust size: For smaller head (18-20"), make 34 rows wide instead of 38 (about 16.5" flat). For larger head (22-23"), make 42 rows wide (about 20" flat). Height stays 32 chains for 10", chain 28 for shorter beanie (9"), chain 36 for taller slouchy (11").
  • Gauge: With 8mm hook and super chunky, 7 hdc = 4 inches wide, 6 rows = 4 inches tall. Don't stress about exact gauge — this beanie is very forgiving.
Beginner check: After 10 rows, measure your width. It should be about 4.75 inches. If it's way off (like 6 inches), your tension is loose — try going down to 7mm hook. If it's 3.5 inches, go up to 9mm. Chunky yarn shows tension fast.

Abbreviations

US terms, very simple:

  • ch — chain
  • hdc — half double crochet
  • sl st — slip stitch
  • st(s) — stitch(es)
  • BLO — back loop only (we use this for a little ribbed look at brim, optional)

Full roadmap — 5 steps

Whole Halloween beanie at a glance — rectangle method:

Step 1: Chain 32 with black yarn (10 inches tall) — foundation chain
Step 2: Rows 1-38: hdc across (31 sts) — 4 rows black, 4 rows pumpkin, repeat. Ends at 18 inches wide
Step 3: Fold rectangle in half, seam the 10-inch side to make a tube — this tube is your beanie body
Step 4: Cinch top closed — weave tapestry needle through top edge stitches and pull tight to close crown
Step 5: Weave ends, add optional tiny bat, shape and wear

38 rows total: 8 + 4 (thumb? no thumb here) — just 38 straight. No math trick, no gaps. Seam one side, close top. Beginner proof.

Step-by-step with photos

1 Foundation chain — the height

With black super chunky yarn and 8mm hook, chain 32. Keep it loose and even — wiggle your hook a bit after each chain. Lay it flat and measure — should be about 10 inches. This chain is the height of your beanie from brim edge up to crown. Don't twist it.

Beginner tip: Place a marker in your first chain you made — it helps you find it when you come back for row 1. Count your chains twice.

2 First rows — building the width

Row 1: hdc in 2nd chain from hook and across. You should have 31 hdc. Chain 1, turn. (31 sts)

Row 2: hdc across — 31 hdc. Chain 1, turn. Still black yarn.

Continue for 4 rows total in black. At end of row 4, switch to pumpkin orange — just pull orange through last yarn over of last hdc.

How to switch colors: On last hdc of black row, yarn over, pull through first two loops, then yarn over with new orange color and pull through last two loops. Cut black, leave 6-inch tail to weave later.

3 Body — stripe pattern to 38 rows

Rows 5-8: With pumpkin orange, hdc across 31 sts, ch1 turn. 4 rows pumpkin.

Rows 9-12: Switch to black, hdc across 4 rows.

Keep repeating 4 black, 4 orange until you have 38 rows total. End with 2 rows black if you want brim and crown both black like mine. My order: 4 black, 4 orange, 4 black, 4 orange, 4 black, 4 orange, 4 black, 4 orange, 4 black, 2 black = 38 rows.

Measure width now: should be about 18 inches. If it's 17, that's okay — chunky stretches. If it's 20, your tension is loose and beanie will be slouchy larger — still wearable, just note for next time.

4 Seam into tube — side seam

Lay rectangle flat, with right side facing you (the prettier side). Fold it in half so the first row meets the last row — you are folding along the width, bringing the two 10-inch edges together. The chain edge and the opposite edge are now both at top and bottom? No — when folded this way, the top edge (10 inch) and bottom edge (10 inch) are open, and the side you are seaming is the 10-inch height. Use tapestry needle and black yarn to whip stitch or mattress stitch the side closed from brim to crown. Seam all the way up — 32 stitches seamed.

After seaming, turn tube so seam is inside if you want hidden seam, or leave outside for a design detail — I leave mine inside. You now have a tube that is 10 inches tall and about 19 inches around.

5 Close the crown — cinch top

With tapestry needle and long tail (about 20 inches) of black yarn, weave needle in and out through every other stitch around the top edge of the tube. Go all the way around the 31 stitches. Pull tight like a drawstring — the top will gather closed. Go around again for strength, pull tight, knot, weave tail inside.

Flip beanie right side out, poke crown with finger to shape. Weave in all tails — black and orange stripe tails — going back and forth a few times so they don't pop out.

6 Final — optional bat and shaping

For the little bat like in the pin: with scrap black and 4mm hook, ch 4, sl st, make tiny wings with 2 hdc each side, or just use felt bats from craft store like in your pin. Sew bat to side of beanie with tapestry needle, about 2 inches above brim.

Try on, stretch brim over ears, fold brim up once if you like a folded brim look — I fold mine up about 2 inches for extra warmth.

How I finish mine for Halloween

After weaving ends, I steam block just a tiny bit — hold steamer 6 inches away, not touching, just to relax stitches. For photos like your pin, I place beanie on cream linen with mini pumpkins, white pumpkins, cinnamon bundles, dried orange slices, pinecones, and a couple felt bats. I like morning light from window on left side, wooden table background — same as your pin that you said was fire.

I fold brim up 2 inches for photos so stripes show nicely. If you made bat, sew it on after blocking. Fluff crown with fingers.

Ways to make it your own

  • Color play: Black + cream + orange, solid black with orange bat, purple + black for spooky witchy, or oatmeal + rust for non-Halloween fall beanie that matches your ear warmer.
  • Bat or no bat: Without bat it's still perfect Halloween colors. With small felt bats, ghost, or pumpkin applique — all cute.
  • Matching set: Make matching twisted ear warmer in same black/orange stripes and fingerless gloves — I did this set and it sold fast at market.
  • Slouchy version: Chain 36 instead of 32 for taller 11-inch slouchy beanie — same 38 rows wide.
  • Kid size: Chain 28 (9 inches tall) and 32 rows wide (15.5 inches flat) for child 18-19 inch head.

Troubleshooting — common beginner fixes

  • Foundation chain too tight, brim won't stretch? Re-chain with 9mm hook, keep loose. Or chain 34 instead of 32 for extra give.
  • Rectangle curling? Super chunky curls a bit at first — after 10 rows it flattens. Tug gently at corners. Blocking after helps too.
  • Lost count of rows? Count the ridges — each row is a ridge. Or count stripes: each color block is 4 rows, so 9 blocks = 36 rows, plus 2 = 38. Place marker every 10 rows.
  • Seam is bulky? Use mattress stitch instead of whip stitch, or seam with thinner black yarn (worsted) held double — less bulk for chunky.
  • Crown has hole after cinching? Go around second time with needle, pull tighter, weave tail through gathered stitches in star pattern, knot inside.
  • Beanie too big/small? Too big (22"+ relaxed) — next time do 34 rows. Too small (under 18" relaxed) — do 42 rows. Height adjust with chain count, not rows.
  • Color jog when switching? Always switch on last yarn over of last stitch of row, not after. Carry yarn up side loosely if same color comes back in 8 rows — don't cut every time if you want less ends.

Caring for your beanie

Hand wash gently in cool water with mild soap, squeeze not wring, lay flat to dry. Chunky acrylic is forgiving. If you used wool blend, lay flat and reshape crown while damp. Remove bat before washing if felt bat, or hand wash bat gently if crochet bat. Fluff with fingers after dry.

Store folded, not hanging, so it keeps shape. Keeps for many Halloweens.
